title: Chapter 10 — Parties In The United States
paragraphs: A great distinction must be drawn between parties. Some countries are so large that the different populations within them have contradictory interests, even though they are subjects of the same government, and they may therefore be in a perpetual state of opposition. In such a case the different fractions of the people should more properly be regarded as distinct nations than as mere parties. If a civil war breaks out, the struggle is carried on by rival peoples rather than by factions within a single state.

But when the citizens hold different opinions on subjects that affect the whole country alike — such as the principles on which the government is to be run — then distinctions arise that may correctly be called parties. Parties are a necessary evil in free governments, but they do not always have the same character and the same tendencies.

At certain times a nation may be oppressed by such unbearable evils that it conceives the idea of a total change in its political constitution. At other times the mischief lies still deeper, and the existence of society itself is endangered. These are the times of great revolutions and of great parties. But between these epochs of misery and confusion there are periods during which human society seems to rest and humanity seems to take a pause. This pause is really only apparent, for time does not stop its course for nations any more than for men. They are all moving toward a goal they do not know, and we only imagine them to be motionless when their progress escapes our observation — just as men walking at a slow pace seem to be standing still to those who are running.

However that may be, there are certain periods in which the changes that take place in the social and political constitution of nations are so slow and so imperceptible that men imagine their present state to be final. The human mind, believing itself firmly based on certain foundations, does not push its investigations beyond the horizon it can see. These are the times of small parties and of intrigue.

The political parties I call great are those that cling to principles more than to consequences, to general rather than particular cases, to ideas rather than men. These parties are usually marked by a nobler character, by more generous passions, by more genuine convictions, and by a bolder and more open conduct than the others. In them, private interest — which always plays the chief part in political passions — is more carefully veiled under the pretext of the public good, and it may sometimes be hidden even from the eyes of those whom it excites and drives.

Minor parties, on the other hand, are generally deficient in political faith. As they are not sustained or ennobled by any lofty purpose, they openly display the selfishness of their character in their actions. They burn with a manufactured zeal; their language is vehement, but their conduct is timid and irresolute. The means they use are as wretched as the ends they aim at. That is why, when a calm state of affairs follows a violent revolution, the leaders of society seem suddenly to disappear and the powers of the human mind to lie hidden. Society is convulsed by great parties; it is agitated by minor ones. It is torn by the former and degraded by the latter. If the great parties sometimes save it by a salutary shock, the minor ones invariably disturb it to no good end.

America has already lost the great parties that once divided the nation. Though her happiness has been considerably increased, her morality has suffered by their extinction. When the War of Independence ended and the foundations of the new government were to be laid, the nation was divided between two opinions — two opinions as old as the world, which are perpetually to be met with under all the forms and names that have ever existed in free communities. One of them tended to limit, the other to extend indefinitely, the power of the people. The conflict of these two opinions never took on, in America, the degree of violence it has frequently shown elsewhere. Both American parties were, in fact, agreed on the most essential points, and neither had to destroy a traditional constitution or overthrow the structure of society in order to guarantee its own triumph. In neither of them, consequently, were a great many private interests affected by success or failure. But moral principles of a high order — such as the love of equality and independence — were at stake in the struggle, and they were enough to kindle violent passions.

The party that wanted to limit the power of the people tried to apply its doctrines above all to the Constitution of the Union, from which it took the name Federal. The other party, which claimed to be more exclusively attached to the cause of liberty, took the name Republican. America is a land of democracy, and the Federalists were always in a minority. But they counted on their side almost all the great men brought forward by the War of Independence, and their moral influence was very considerable. Their cause was also favored by circumstances. The ruin of the Confederation had filled the people with a dread of anarchy, and the Federalists did not fail to make use of this temporary disposition of the multitude. For ten or twelve years they were at the head of affairs and were able to apply some, though not all, of their principles; for the hostile current was growing daily too violent to be checked or resisted. In 1801 the Republicans took control of the government. Thomas Jefferson was chosen President, and he strengthened the influence of their party by the weight of his celebrity, the greatness of his talents, and the immense extent of his popularity.

The means by which the Federalists had kept their position were artificial, and their resources were temporary. It was by the virtues or the talents of their leaders that they had risen to power. When the Republicans reached that lofty station, their opponents were overwhelmed by utter defeat. An immense majority declared itself against the outgoing party, and the Federalists found themselves in so small a minority that they at once despaired of ever succeeding again. From that moment the Republican, or Democratic, party*a has gone from conquest to conquest, until it has acquired absolute supremacy in the country. The Federalists, seeing that they were beaten beyond recovery and isolated in the midst of the nation, split into two groups. One joined the victorious Republicans; the other abandoned its rallying point and its name. Many years have now passed since they ceased to exist as a party.

a [[It is hardly necessary to remark that in more recent times the meaning of these terms has changed. The Republicans are the representatives of the old Federalists, and the Democrats of the old Republicans. — Trans. Note (1861).]] The accession of the Federalists to power was, in my opinion, one of the most fortunate incidents that accompanied the formation of the great American Union. They resisted the inevitable tendencies of their age and of their country. But whether their theories were good or bad, they had the defect of being inapplicable, as a system, to the society they claimed to govern, and what occurred under Jefferson's auspices was therefore bound to happen sooner or later. But their government gave the new republic time to acquire a certain stability, and afterwards to support the rapid growth of the very doctrines they had combated. A considerable number of their principles were in fact embodied in the political creed of their opponents, and the Federal Constitution that still exists today is a lasting monument to their patriotism and their wisdom.

Great political parties, then, are not to be met with in the United States at the present time. Parties do exist that threaten the future tranquility of the Union, but there are none that seem to contest the present form of government or the present course of society. The parties that menace the Union do not rest on abstract principles, but on material interests. These interests, spread across the provinces of so vast an empire, may be said to form rival nations rather than rival parties. Thus, on a recent occasion, the North argued for a system of commercial prohibition and the South took up arms in favor of free trade, simply because the North is a manufacturing district and the South an agricultural one, and the restrictive system that benefited the one was harmful to the other.*b

b [[The divisions of North and South have since gained a far greater intensity, and the South, though conquered, still presents a formidable spirit of opposition to Northern government. — Translator's Note, 1875.]]

In the absence of great parties, the United States abounds with lesser controversies, and public opinion is divided into a thousand minute shades of difference on questions of very little importance. The pains taken to create parties are inconceivable, and at present it is no easy task. In the United States there is no religious animosity, because all religion is respected and no sect is predominant. There is no jealousy of rank, because the people is everything and no one can contest its authority. And lastly, there is no public destitution to provide the fuel for agitation, because the physical situation of the country opens so wide a field to industry that a man can accomplish the most surprising undertakings with his own native resources. Nevertheless, ambitious men have an interest in the creation of parties, since it is hard to remove a person from office on the mere ground that his place is coveted by others. The skill of the actors in the political world therefore consists in the art of creating parties. A political aspirant in the United States begins by identifying his own interest and calculating what interests can be gathered around it and joined with it. He then contrives to find some doctrine or principle that will suit the purposes of this new association, and which he adopts in order to put forward his party and secure his popularity. In much the same way, a king's imprimatur was formerly bound into the volume it authorized, though it did not really belong to the book at all. When these preliminaries are complete, the new party is ushered into the political world.

All the domestic controversies of the Americans at first appear to a stranger so incomprehensible and so childish that he is at a loss whether to pity a people that takes such trifles seriously or to envy the happiness that allows it to discuss them. But when he comes to study the secret tendencies that govern the factions of America, he easily sees that most of them are more or less connected with one or the other of those two divisions that have always existed in free communities. The deeper we look into the workings of these parties, the more clearly we see that the object of the one is to limit the popular authority, and that of the other to extend it. I do not claim that the declared aim, or even the secret aim, of American parties is to promote the rule of aristocracy or democracy in the country. But I do affirm that aristocratic or democratic passions may easily be detected at the bottom of every party, and that although they escape a superficial observation, they are the main point and the very soul of every faction in the United States.

To give a recent example: when the President attacked the Bank, the country was stirred up and parties formed. The well-informed classes rallied to the Bank, the common people to the President. But it must not be imagined that the people had formed a rational opinion on a question that presents so many difficulties even to the most experienced statesmen. The Bank is a great institution with an independent existence of its own, and the people, accustomed to making and unmaking whatever it pleases, is startled to meet such an obstacle to its authority. In the midst of the constant flux of society, the community is irritated by so permanent an institution and is led to attack it, to see whether it can be shaken and controlled like all the other institutions of the country.
Remains Of The Aristocratic Party In The United States

Secret opposition of wealthy individuals to democracy — Their retirement — Their taste for exclusive pleasures and for luxury at home — Their simplicity in public — Their affected condescension toward the people.

It sometimes happens among a people in which various opinions prevail that the balance between the several parties is lost, and one of them gains an irresistible preponderance, overcomes all obstacles, harasses its opponents, and appropriates all the resources of society to its own purposes. The defeated citizens despair of success and conceal their dissatisfaction in silence and general apathy. The nation seems to be governed by a single principle, and the ruling party takes credit for restoring peace and unanimity to the country. But this apparent unanimity is merely a cloak for alarming dissensions and perpetual opposition.

This is exactly what happened in America. When the democratic party gained the upper hand, it took exclusive possession of the conduct of affairs, and from that time on the laws and customs of society have been shaped to fit its whims. Today the more prosperous classes of society are so entirely removed from the direction of political affairs in the United States that wealth, far from conferring a right to exercise power, is more an obstacle than a means to it. The wealthy members of the community leave the field, unwilling to contend, and often to contend in vain, against the poorest classes of their fellow citizens. They concentrate all their enjoyments in the privacy of their homes, where they occupy a rank that cannot be claimed in public. They form a private society within the state, with its own tastes and its own pleasures. They submit to this situation as an irremediable evil, but they are careful not to show that they chafe under it. It is even not uncommon to hear them extolling, in public, the charms of republican government and the advantages of democratic institutions. Next to hating their enemies, men are most inclined to flatter them.

Notice, for example, that wealthy citizen who is as anxious to hide his wealth as a Jew of the Middle Ages. His dress is plain, his manner unassuming. But the interior of his home glitters with luxury, and only a few chosen guests — whom he haughtily calls his equals — are allowed into this sanctuary. No European noble is more exclusive in his pleasures or more jealous of the smallest privileges his station confers. But the very same man crosses the city to reach a dark counting-house in the center of the business district, where anyone who pleases may come up and speak to him. If he meets his cobbler on the way, they stop and talk. The two citizens discuss the affairs of the state, in which they have an equal stake, and they shake hands before parting.

But beneath this manufactured enthusiasm and these obsequious attentions to the dominant power, it is easy to see that the wealthy members of the community harbor a hearty distaste for the democratic institutions of their country. The populace is at once the object of their scorn and of their fears. If the mismanagement of the democracy ever brings about a revolutionary crisis, and if monarchical institutions ever become practicable in the United States, the truth of what I am saying will become obvious.
The two main weapons parties use to secure success are the public press and the formation of associations.
